facts.title: Once Pricier Than Gold
facts.text: In the mid-19th century aluminium was so hard to isolate that it was considered a precious metal. Napoleon III reportedly reserved aluminium cutlery for his most honored guests while lesser visitors made do with gold. At the 1855 Paris Exposition, bars of aluminium were displayed beside the French crown jewels.

facts.title: Named for Alum
facts.text: The name comes from 'alumen', the Latin word for alum, a compound used by Greeks and Romans for dyeing and as a styptic. Humphry Davy proposed the name 'alumium' in 1808, then revised it to 'aluminum'; British editors later standardized 'aluminium' to match elements like sodium and potassium. Both spellings remain in use today, with 'aluminum' favored in North America.

facts.title: Most Abundant Metal in the Crust
facts.text: Aluminium makes up about 8.2% of Earth's crust by mass, making it the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element overall after oxygen and silicon. Despite this, it is never found as a pure metal in nature because it bonds so eagerly with oxygen. It occurs locked inside minerals such as feldspars, micas, and the ore bauxite.

facts.title: The Hall-Heroult Breakthrough
facts.text: In 1886, 22-year-old American Charles Martin Hall and Frenchman Paul Heroult independently discovered the same way to extract aluminium using electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite. This process slashed the price of aluminium from a luxury metal to an everyday material within a few years. The Hall-Heroult process still produces essentially all the world's primary aluminium today.

facts.title: It Wears Invisible Armor
facts.text: Although aluminium is highly reactive, a freshly exposed surface instantly forms a thin, transparent layer of aluminium oxide only a few nanometers thick. This self-healing film is tough and tightly bonded, protecting the metal underneath from further corrosion. This is why aluminium pans, foil, and aircraft skins resist rust so well even though the metal itself is chemically eager to react.

facts.title: Recycling Saves 95% of the Energy
facts.text: Smelting aluminium from ore is enormously energy-intensive, but recycling used aluminium requires only about 5% of that energy. A discarded drink can be melted down, reformed, refilled, and back on a shelf in as little as 60 days. Roughly 75% of all aluminium ever produced is estimated to still be in use thanks to this near-infinite recyclability.

facts.title: Light Enough to Fly
facts.text: With a density of about 2.7 grams per cubic centimeter, aluminium is roughly one-third the weight of steel, which is why it became the backbone of aviation and spaceflight. Alloyed with copper, magnesium, or zinc, it gains the strength needed for aircraft fuselages, rockets, and satellites. The Wright brothers used an aluminium engine block in 1903 because no other strong, light metal was available.

facts.title: A Gemstone in Disguise
facts.text: Pure aluminium oxide is the mineral corundum, and tiny traces of other elements turn it into famous gemstones. A pinch of chromium makes it a red ruby, while iron and titanium produce blue sapphire. Synthetic corundum is also one of the hardest materials made, ranking 9 on the Mohs scale just below diamond.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: The aluminium in your soda can was created inside massive stars through nuclear fusion, particularly during the carbon and neon burning stages near the end of a star's life. A radioactive form, aluminium-26, glows in gamma rays across our galaxy and helped heat the earliest rocky bodies in the young Solar System. Detecting this isotope lets astronomers map where new stars are currently forming in the Milky Way.

facts.title: No Job in the Human Body
facts.text: Unlike iron, calcium, or zinc, aluminium has no known biological function in humans and is not needed by any living cell. The body absorbs very little of what we eat, and healthy kidneys efficiently filter out the rest. Plants, however, can suffer from aluminium toxicity in acidic soils, where the dissolved metal stunts root growth and limits crop yields worldwide.
